```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.path = "figures/", dpi = 110, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4)
library(zoo)
library(car)
source("dcs_t.R")
```

A comparison of a Gaussian **ARIMA(1,1,0)** with a robust **Student-t score-driven (DCS-t) model** for the monthly Global Price of Uranium (IMF, via FRED series [PURANUSDM](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PURANUSDM)), January 1992 – March 2026.

*Coursework for Advanced Time Series, MSc in Statistical Sciences, University of Bologna, by **Alessandro Baroni, Mohammadmahdi Ameridaragheh and Leonardo Bizzotto**. This repository is a cleaned-up, fully reproducible version: the DCS-t filter and estimator in [`dcs_t.R`](dcs_t.R) are a fresh implementation, and estimation now uses multiple starting points (see [Note on estimation](#note-on-estimation)).*

## Why a score-driven model?

Uranium is a thin, contract-driven market. A few events (the 2006 Cigar Lake mine flood, the 2011 Fukushima accident, the 2021 launch of the Sprott Physical Uranium Trust and the 2022 invasion of Ukraine) have moved the price by tens of dollars per pound within months. The result is a non-stationary series with volatility clustering and very heavy-tailed changes, which is exactly where a Gaussian filter struggles.

A DCS model updates the latent mean with the **score** of the conditional density instead of the raw prediction error $v_t = y_t - \mu_t$. Under a Student-t density, that score is

$$u_t = \frac{v_t}{1 + v_t^2/(\nu\varsigma)}, \qquad \mu_{t+1} = \omega + \phi(\mu_t - \omega) + \kappa u_t .$$

It behaves like $v_t$ for small errors but is bounded and *redescending*, so extreme observations are automatically downweighted (Harvey, 2013; Creal, Koopman & Lucas, 2013).

## Data

```{r data, fig.height = 5.5}
d   <- read.csv("PURANUSDM.csv")
y   <- zoo(d$PURANUSDM, as.Date(d$observation_date))
obs <- as.numeric(y)
c(n = length(obs), missing = sum(is.na(obs)))

par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(y, xlab = "", ylab = "USD per lb")
plot(diff(y), xlab = "", ylab = "Monthly change"); abline(h = 0, col = "grey60", lty = 2)
```

The level peaks at about `r round(max(obs))` USD/lb in mid-2007, almost twenty times its 1992 value. In levels, the ACF decays slowly and the PACF has a single spike at lag 1. That points to a unit root, so the benchmark is fitted to the first differences. The monthly changes show two clear turbulent regimes: 2006–2008 and after 2020.

## Benchmark: ARIMA(1,1,0)

```{r arima, fig.height = 6}
arima_fit <- arima(obs, order = c(1, 1, 0), method = "ML")
arima_fit
res_arima <- residuals(arima_fit)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(res_arima, type = "l", main = "ARIMA residuals", ylab = "", xlab = "Month")
acf(res_arima, main = "Residual ACF")
plot(density(res_arima), main = "Density vs Normal")
curve(dnorm(x, mean(res_arima), sd(res_arima)), add = TRUE, col = "orange", lty = 2)
qqPlot(res_arima, main = "Normal Q-Q", ylab = "", id = FALSE)
shapiro.test(res_arima)
```

The ARIMA takes care of the linear memory: its residual ACF is mostly inside the bands. But the residuals are heavily leptokurtic and show volatility clustering, and Shapiro–Wilk rejects normality (p < 0.001). The Gaussian likelihood is the wrong tool for this series.

## DCS-t model

```{r dcs}
fit <- dcs_t_fit_multistart(obs, n_starts = 60)
round(fit$theta, 3)
filt <- dcs_t_filter(obs, fit$theta)
```

```{r dcs-filter}
plot(obs, type = "l", col = "grey40", xlab = "Month", ylab = "USD per lb",
     main = "Observed price and DCS-t filtered mean")
lines(filt$mu, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
legend("topleft", c("Observed", "DCS-t filtered mean"), col = c("grey40", "firebrick"),
       lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

```{r dcs-score}
plot(filt$v, type = "l", ylab = "", xlab = "Month",
     main = "Prediction errors and score innovations")
lines(filt$u, col = "steelblue", lwd = 1.5)
legend("topleft", c(expression(v[t] ~ "(prediction error)"), expression(u[t] ~ "(score)")),
       col = c("black", "steelblue"), lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

The score clips the extreme errors of 2007 and 2021–2022: the largest prediction error is `r round(max(abs(filt$v)), 1)` USD/lb, but the largest score innovation is only `r round(max(abs(filt$u)), 1)`. A single shock therefore cannot drag the filtered mean around for months.

The estimates are as follows:

- **φ = `r round(fit$theta["phi"], 3)`:** this is at the edge of stationarity, matching the unit-root behaviour seen in the ACF.
- **κ = `r round(fit$theta["kappa"], 2)`:** once the score has shrunk the outliers, the filter reacts strongly to new information.
- **ν = `r round(fit$theta["nu"], 1)`:** the tails are much heavier than Gaussian (a Gaussian corresponds to ν → ∞).

## Model comparison

```{r compare}
aic <- c("ARIMA(1,1,0)" = arima_fit$aic, "DCS-t" = fit$aic)
round(aic, 1)
```

The DCS-t lowers the AIC by **`r round(aic[1] - aic[2])` points**, far beyond the ΔAIC > 10 rule of thumb (Burnham & Anderson, 2002), despite having three more parameters. The gain comes from three things:

- **Heavy tails:** the Student-t gives far more likelihood to the 2007 and 2021–2022 moves.
- **Robustness:** the bounded score stops one-off shocks from biasing the filter.
- **Adaptive updates:** the filter updates more slowly in turbulent periods and faster in calm ones.

## Note on estimation

The likelihood surface is multimodal, because ω is weakly identified when φ ≈ 1. The original coursework used a single starting point, (0, 0.9, 0.7, 1, 2). From there the optimiser stops at a local optimum with ν ≈ 3.6 and an AIC gap of about 46.

```{r local}
local <- dcs_t_fit(obs, start = c(0, 0.9, 0.7, 1, 2.2))
round(c(local$theta, AIC = local$aic), 3)
```

Restarting from `r length(fit$all_aic)` random points finds a better optimum (AIC `r round(fit$aic, 1)` vs `r round(local$aic, 1)`). This makes the case for the DCS-t even stronger and gives a less extreme ν. The conclusions do not change, but the lesson is a good one: always use multiple starting points for non-linear likelihoods.

The estimator recovers known parameters from simulated data:

```{r sim}
set.seed(1)
true <- c(omega = 10, phi = 0.95, kappa = 0.8, varsigma = 2, nu = 4)
sim  <- dcs_t_simulate(2000, true)
round(rbind(true = true, estimated = dcs_t_fit_multistart(sim$y, 20)$theta), 3)
```

## Possible extensions

- A score-driven recursion for the scale (location and scale DCS-t) to model volatility clustering directly
- Skewed or generalised hyperbolic densities
- A multivariate model linking uranium to other energy commodities

```r
install.packages(c("zoo", "car", "rmarkdown"))
rmarkdown::render("README.Rmd")
```
